lead: There are two ways to stretch the tendon. In pre-tensioning the tendon is stretched first and the concrete is cast around it; in post-tensioning the concrete is cast first with a duct inside, and the tendon is stretched after the concrete has hardened. The order decides how the force enters the concrete: by bond along the tendon in pre-tensioning, through end anchorages in post-tensioning. Only a few universities teach the systems in detail, so this chapter is short.
prereq: You need the idea of transfer and the wires and strands used as tendons.

blocks.text: The tendons are stretched between two heavy abutments at the ends of a casting bed and held by grips. Moulds are set round them, concrete is cast and cured, often with steam so that it gains strength in a day. When the concrete reaches its transfer strength, the tendons are released slowly from the abutments or cut. Each tendon tries to shorten, the concrete grips it, and the force passes into the concrete by bond over a short transmission length at each end. No anchorage is left in the member.

In the long-line method (Hoyer system) one bed, often 100 m or more, holds many units end to end, and one stressing operation serves them all: railway sleepers, poles, piles and hollow-core slabs are made this way. The tendons are usually straight; they can be deflected (harped) at hold-down points to follow the moment, but sharp curves are not possible. It needs a factory, and units must be transportable.

A duct (corrugated steel or plastic sheath) is fixed in the formwork to the planned profile, and the concrete is cast. After it hardens, the tendon is threaded through, stressed by a jack that pushes against the concrete face, and locked by an anchorage that bears on the concrete through a plate. The duct is then filled with cement grout, which protects the steel and bonds it to the concrete. Curved profiles are easy, which suits continuous beams, long bridge girders and site-cast slabs.

Systems differ in how they grip the tendon. Freyssinet uses a conical male wedge in a female cone to grip a ring of wires or strands. Magnel-Blaton grips pairs of wires in sandwich plates with flat wedges. Gifford-Udall anchors each wire with split cone wedges in a barrel. Lee-McCall stresses threaded high-tensile bars and locks them with nuts. Modern multi-strand systems use a wedge plate with one tapered three-piece wedge per strand.

examples.question: A post-tensioned tendon of 7 strands of 12.7 mm (98.7 mm² each), 30 m long, is jacked to 1395 N/mm². E<sub>s</sub> = 195 kN/mm². (a) Find the jack force and the extension the jack must give. (b) The wedges draw in 6 mm at lock-off. Find the stress lost, ignoring friction. (c) Compare a single strand in a 100 m pre-tensioning bed with the same 6 mm draw-in.
steps: Extension Δ = f L/E<sub>s</sub> = 1395 × 30,000/195,000 = 214.6 mm. Site staff check the measured extension against it.
(b) Stress lost = E<sub>s</sub> δ/L = 195,000 × 6/30,000 = 39 N/mm², 2.8 percent of the jacking stress.
examples.answer: Jack force 963.8 kN with an extension of 214.6 mm; a 6 mm draw-in costs 39 N/mm² (2.8 percent) in the 30 m tendon but only 11.7 N/mm² in a 100 m bed, which is one reason long-line beds work well.

traps: Saying post-tensioning transfers force by bond. The anchorage transfers it at stressing; grout gives bond only later.
Saying grouting stresses the tendon. Grout protects and bonds a tendon that is already stressed.
Treating a coupler as an anchorage. A coupler joins two tendon lengths.

quiz.q: Define pre-tensioning and post-tensioning in one line each.
quiz.a: Pre-tensioning: tendons stressed before casting and released after hardening, force by bond. Post-tensioning: concrete cast with ducts, tendons stressed after hardening, force by end anchorages.

quiz.q: Why does pre-tensioning need no end anchorage in the member?
quiz.a: After release the tendon is held by bond with the hardened concrete over the transmission length at each end.

quiz.q: A 40 m tendon is jacked to 1400 N/mm² with E<sub>s</sub> = 195 kN/mm². Find the extension.
Which system would you choose for a continuous three-span cast-in-place bridge, and why?
quiz.a: Post-tensioning: the curved tendon profile can follow the moment over the supports, the girders are too large to transport, and couplers allow staged construction.

beyond: Not for the exam. Precast segmental bridges, such as many metro viaducts, are post-tensioned through match-cast segments. Long-line plants now use self-compacting concrete and automatic strand cutting. Search for precast segmental construction and hollow-core slab production.

figure.caption: Pre-tensioning stretches the tendon between abutments before casting; post-tensioning stresses it through a duct in hardened concrete and anchors it at the ends. The extensions are those of the worked example.
